title: The ministers' arguments
hookLine: the king's ministers come to bring him home, with every argument they have (Buddhacarita 9)

cards: Your father is burning with grief. That's the opening line of the case, more or less, and it's delivered by two men who have walked a long way to say it.
The king can't go himself, so he sends his family priest and his minister, with one job: bring the prince home. They find him resting under a tree. They bow.
And then they begin, and they've come prepared.

teach.b: First, the heart. The priest speaks for the family: your father's grief, the queen who raised you, your wife, your small son. Come back for them.
You can practice what is right at home, as a king. Kings of old found freedom while they still ruled. There will be time for the forest later, when you're old and the throne has passed on.
Third, the doubt. The minister tries a different road.

Who really knows what comes after death? Some teachers say there's another life, some say there isn't. Some say things simply happen by their own nature, the way a thorn is sharp without anyone sharpening it.
Why give up everything for a question no one can settle? Love, duty, tradition, and doubt itself: they use every argument they have. Fourth, the answer.
The prince hears each man out and answers each in turn. In paraphrase, he tells the priest he knows his father's love, and it grieves him, but parting will come anyway, by death if not by this.

To the minister he says he won't take this question secondhand, from whichever teacher sounds surest. He'll find out for himself. He would sooner walk into fire than go home with his search unfinished.
He stands and walks on, and the two men go home slowly, the poem says, looking back.
Udayin argued from pleasure. These two argue from love, and then from doubt. And to doubt, the prince doesn't answer with a certainty of his own.

how: Buddhist communities teach the prince's resolve in this scene as an example of determination, and in some communities the story of family members asking a renunciant to come home is part of how people talk about ordination and the families of monks and nuns.

o: a lack of courage to follow your choice
a sin that blocks the way to heaven
not knowing for sure what comes after death

games.q: the arguments, and who makes them: tap the pairs.
p: asks who really knows what comes after

s: in the poem, the king rides out himself to bring his son home
he sends his family priest and his minister.
one of the arguments is that no one can be sure what comes after death
the minister uses doubt itself as a reason to go home.
the prince loses patience and sends them away angrily
he hears them out, answers kindly, and walks on.

games.q: you're the prince. two wise men from your father's court have given you every reason to come home: love, duty, tradition, and doubt. what do you do?
o: go home for your father's sake.
argue until they agree with you.
games.why: he says he knows his father's love, that parting comes anyway, and that he won't settle the deepest question secondhand. he'd sooner walk into fire than go home unfinished.

practice: Bring to mind a time someone pushed you hard to change your mind, and notice where the pressure shows up in your body, the jaw, the shoulders, the chest; breathe into that place.

Then picture yourself the way the prince sits under the tree, hearing each point, not raising your voice, not folding. Let your feet press into the floor, and feel how steady the ground stays under all that talk.

wordCard.voice: doubt. What the king's minister raises against the prince's leaving, since no one can prove what comes after death; the prince answers not with certainty, but with a search. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: every argument. If no one can settle it, he'll go and look. Day seven hundred ten.
